title: ICU and Continuous EEG
subtitle: Decode the order, know why the EEG is there, record it well, and test reactivity safely

tabs.title: Overview
tabs.intro: Continuous EEG (cEEG) in the ICU is a long recording, usually with video, in patients who cannot tell you what is happening in their brain. Most ICU seizures are nonconvulsive, so the EEG is often the only way to see them. Your first job is to read the order and work out what question the team wants the EEG to answer.

cards.title: Find hidden seizures
cards.body: Detect nonconvulsive seizures (NCS) and nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) in patients with altered mental status or coma.
points: Main and strongest indication in the ACNS consensus
A 30 to 60 minute routine EEG misses many NCS

cards.title: Guide treatment
cards.body: Show whether seizure treatment is working, and help titrate infusions toward a target the physician sets (for example seizure suppression or burst suppression).

cards.title: Detect ischemia
cards.body: Watch for new slowing and loss of fast activity in patients at high risk of stroke, such as after subarachnoid hemorrhage when vasospasm can cause delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI).

cards.title: Track sedation and coma depth
cards.body: Show the depth of sedation or pharmacological coma, especially when the patient is paralyzed and cannot be examined.

cards.title: Describe severity and support prognosis
cards.body: Background continuity, reactivity and patterns are used by the physician to grade encephalopathy and, for example, after cardiac arrest. The technologist records and describes; the physician interprets.

cards.title: Characterize events
cards.body: Capture twitching, posturing, eye deviation or vital-sign spikes on video and EEG to decide whether they are seizures.

sections.title: Who orders it and who is involved
items: Ordered by the treating team: neurocritical care, neurology, neurosurgery, intensivists, pediatric or neonatal teams, often after a neurology consult.
The neurodiagnostic technologist (NDT) sets up, maintains quality, tests reactivity, marks events, screens trends and notifies per protocol.
The electroencephalographer (EEG reader) interprets, reports at least daily, and gives interim calls for important changes.
The bedside nurse (RN) presses the event button, reports clinical events, and is your partner for skin, positioning, stimulation and safety.
Respiratory therapy, perfusion (ECMO) and dialysis staff own devices that can produce artifact; know who to ask.

sections.title: How to read an ICU order
items: Identify the main diagnosis and injury (for example SAH, TBI, HIE after cardiac arrest).
Find the timeline: hospital day, post-op day (POD), post-bleed day, time since ROSC. Timing tells you the risk window.
Note the severity: GCS, Hunt-Hess, FOUR score, RASS. A low GCS or deep RASS means you cannot rely on the clinical exam.
List devices: EVD, ICP monitor, craniotomy or craniectomy site, ECMO, CRRT, cooling. These change electrode placement and artifact.
List drugs: sedatives and their infusion rates (gtt), antiseizure medications, paralytics. These change the EEG and reactivity testing.
Read the question: 'r/o NCSE', 'DCI surveillance', 'titrate to burst suppression', 'prognosis post-arrest', 'characterize events'.
Translate it into what you must do: full montage, special electrode positions, video framing, stimulation testing, which trends to watch, what triggers a call.

sections.title: Worked decoding example
head: Order fragment
Meaning
What it means at the EEG
rows: 71F, HD 3, s/p L crani for acute SDH evacuation, POD 1
Hospital day 3; status post left craniotomy to remove an acute subdural hematoma; first day after surgery
Fresh left surgical site and dressing: no electrodes on the incision, substitute or omit positions and document. Breach effect (sharper, faster activity) over the skull defect is expected.
Glasgow Coma Scale 7 with T meaning intubated (verbal not testable); deeply sedated on a propofol drip
Exam is poor, so seizures could be silent. Propofol slows and may suppress the background; note the rate at hookup and each change.
LEV 1 g IV BID, h/o EtOH use
Levetiracetam 1 gram intravenously twice daily; history of alcohol use
Already on an antiseizure medication; alcohol history raises risk of withdrawal and seizures. Record the drug and dose times.
L gaze deviation x2 per RN
Nurse saw left eye deviation twice
Frame the face on video, ask the RN to press the event button and describe events. Eye leads help.
cEEG to r/o NCSE, MRI planned
Continuous EEG to rule out nonconvulsive status epilepticus; MRI coming
Main question is seizures. Use CT/MRI-compatible electrodes per policy, at least 24 h, notify reader per protocol of any possible seizure.
sections.note: Invented example for teaching. The technologist translates the order into a recording plan; the reader decides what the EEG shows.

pearls: Most seizures in critically ill patients are nonconvulsive, so they are invisible without EEG.
Read the order for four things: diagnosis, timing, devices, drugs. Then the question.
'T' after a GCS (for example 7T) means intubated; the verbal score cannot be tested.
A fresh craniotomy or craniectomy changes electrode placement and causes breach rhythm; document both.
Technologist scope: record, test, mark, describe, notify per protocol. Never diagnose or give prognosis to the family or team.
Write the sedative, paralytic and antiseizure doses at hookup; the reader needs them to interpret the record.
tabs.eegLink: Every set-up choice (electrode type, positions, video framing, stimulation, which trends you watch) should come from the question in the order.

tabs.title: ICU Abbreviations
tabs.intro: ICU orders and charts are dense with shorthand. Each table gives the abbreviation, what it stands for, and why it matters when you are at the EEG machine. Local usage varies, so when an abbreviation is ambiguous, ask.

Meaning

Works in intubated patients because it has no verbal part.

Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU
Delirium screen; delirium is a reason for EEG in some patients.
Hunt and Hess grade for SAH, 1 to 5
Grades 3 to 5 are the high-risk group for DCI surveillance in the ACNS consensus (poor grade usually means 4 to 5) are the high-risk group for DCI surveillance.
World Federation of Neurosurgical Societies SAH grade, 1 to 5 (GCS-based)
Another SAH severity grade; higher means sicker.
Modified Fisher scale, 0 to 4 (blood amount on CT)
Higher grades predict higher vasospasm risk.
Severity and mortality estimate for ICH.
National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale, 0 to 42
Stroke deficit severity; a sudden rise may need EEG to exclude seizure.
Outcome and disability scale used in studies and baseline history.

Meaning

Video lets the reader separate artifact and clinical events.
Umbrella term for prolonged EEG in the ICU or EMU.

Shows power by frequency over time; seizures often appear as bright repeated 'flames'.
Compressed amplitude band; used widely by neonatal teams.

Burst suppression ratio (percent of time suppressed)
Used to track the depth of burst suppression during anesthetic titration.
ESz: epileptiform discharges faster than 2.5 Hz for 10 s or more, or a definite evolving pattern for 10 s or more. ESE: ESz for 10 continuous minutes or 20% of any 60-minute period.
EEG seizure with a time-locked clinical correlate, or EEG and clinical improvement after an IV antiseizure medication.
Patterns that do not meet seizure criteria but may be causing harm; physician decides on treatment.

tabs.title: Indications
tabs.intro: The ACNS consensus statement on continuous EEG in critically ill adults and children (Herman et al., 2015) lists when cEEG is useful and what it is looking for. Recommendations are expert opinion, and each facility writes its own protocol from them.

sections.title: Consensus indications and what the EEG is looking for
head: Indication
Examples
What the EEG is looking for
rows: Persistent abnormal mental status after convulsive SE or clinical seizures
Patient not waking after convulsions stopped
Acute supratentorial brain injury with altered mental status
TBI, ICH, SAH, ischemic stroke, CNS infection, tumor, post-neurosurgery
NCS, periodic and rhythmic patterns, focal changes
Fluctuating or unexplained altered mental status
LPDs, GPDs, BIPDs found on a short study
Whether seizures occur over a longer window
Paralyzed patients, some ECMO and TTM patients
Seizures that cannot be seen clinically
Twitching, posturing, eye deviation, autonomic surges
Whether the events have an EEG correlate
Assessing treatment of seizures and status
Seizure control, breakthrough seizures, depth of suppression
Loss of fast activity, increasing slowing, trend changes
Post cardiac arrest, other comatose patients
Background continuity, voltage, reactivity, patterns; physician interprets

sections.title: Duration and review
items: Start as soon as possible when nonconvulsive seizures are suspected.
At least 24 hours of recording is recommended for seizure screening in most patients.
48 hours or more may be needed in comatose patients, patients with periodic discharges, or sedated patients.
A routine 30 to 60 minute EEG finds NCS in only about half of patients who have them; most are found within 24 to 48 hours.
No epileptiform discharges early in the recording lowers the chance of later seizures, which helps the physician decide when to stop.
The consensus suggests reader review at least twice daily for seizure indications and at least three times daily for vasospasm monitoring; facilities may review more often.

cards.title: Why EEG after arrest
cards.body: Comatose survivors are at high risk of nonconvulsive seizures, and the EEG background is one of several tools the physician uses for prognosis.

cards.title: During cooling and rewarming
cards.body: Sedation, paralytics and low temperature all slow or suppress the EEG. Rewarming is a period when seizures may appear, so keep recording and mark temperature changes.
points: Record temperature, sedation and paralytic status on the record
Shivering produces muscle artifact; note when anti-shivering drugs are given

cards.title: Serial versus continuous
cards.body: The consensus notes that in adults after arrest, brief serial EEGs had similar yield to continuous recording in one study; many centers still use cEEG. Follow facility protocol.

cards.title: Technologist role
cards.body: Perform standardized reactivity testing, describe and mark, notify per protocol. Never comment on prognosis to family or staff.

cards.title: Who and when
cards.body: Highest-risk patients are higher-grade SAH (Hunt-Hess 3 to 5, the group the ACNS consensus flags for DCI surveillance) and those with thick blood on CT. Recording should start before the vasospasm window (about day 3) and continue until it has passed (about day 14).

cards.title: What ischemia looks like
cards.body: First a loss of fast (alpha and beta) activity, then increasing slow (delta) activity. New or worsening focal slowing is a warning sign.

cards.title: Alpha-delta ratio
cards.body: The ratio of alpha power to delta power. A sustained fall, especially regional, can precede clinical DCI. In one small study of poor-grade SAH, a drop of more than 10% from baseline across consecutive measurements, or more than 50% in one measurement, predicted DCI.

cards.title: Relative alpha variability
cards.body: Loss of the normal fluctuation of alpha power over time is another ischemia warning trend.

cards.title: What you do
cards.body: Watch the qEEG trends, check the raw EEG for artifact when a trend drops, and notify the reader per protocol so the team can image or treat.

sections.title: Refractory status and burst-suppression titration
items: The physician sets the EEG goal: seizure suppression, or burst suppression with a target such as interburst interval or BSR.
Record the infusion drugs and rates at baseline and log every bolus and rate change on the record.
Watch the raw EEG and BSR trend; ACNS 2021 defines burst suppression as 50 to 99% of the record suppressed or attenuated, and suppression as voltage under 10 microvolts.
Report breakthrough seizures, bursts that look ictal, or suppression deeper or lighter than the goal, per protocol.
Keep recording through the wean, when seizures often recur, and afterwards for as long as the physician orders.

sections.title: Pediatric and neonatal notes
items: Children, and especially infants, may be at higher risk of nonconvulsive seizures than adults.
Common pediatric indications: after convulsive SE, TBI including abusive head trauma, post-cardiac arrest, ECMO, encephalitis, after cardiac surgery.
Neonates are covered by a separate ACNS guideline. Many neonatal seizures are electrographic only, so clinical observation misses them.
Neonatal HIE treated with therapeutic hypothermia is a main neonatal cEEG indication, usually through cooling and rewarming.
Neonatal teams often use aEEG at the bedside; a full conventional neonatal montage is the reference for confirming seizures.
Use age-appropriate electrode numbers and positions, and gentle skin products: neonatal skin is fragile.

pearls: Strongest consensus indication: finding NCS and NCSE.
At least 24 h for seizure screening; 48 h or more if comatose, sedated or periodic discharges.
SAH vasospasm window: roughly day 3 to day 14 after the bleed.
Ischemia on EEG: fast activity fades first, slowing increases next.
A sustained drop in alpha-delta ratio is a DCI warning sign that must be checked against the raw EEG.
Burst suppression (ACNS 2021) means 50 to 99% of the record is suppressed or attenuated.
Keep recording during rewarming after TTM and during the wean of anesthetic infusions; seizures may appear then.
tabs.eegLink: Knowing the indication tells you which trend to watch, how long to record, and what kind of change needs an urgent call.

tabs.title: Technique and Artifacts
tabs.intro: Long ICU recordings must stay clean for days on patients who are moved, imaged, suctioned and turned. Set-up choices protect both the data and the skin, and good documentation makes the record interpretable.

sections.title: Set-up for long-term ICU recording
items: Verify two identifiers and the order; check allergies (adhesive, collodion, latex) and isolation precautions.
Talk with the RN: drains, incisions, fractures, lines, upcoming imaging or procedures, sedation and paralytics.
Measure and apply a full 10-20 array (a minimum of 16 scalp electrodes per the consensus); reduced or hairline montages are only for rapid screening until the full set can be applied.
Move positions around incisions, drains and bolts, keep left-right symmetry where possible, and document every substitution.
Add ECG at minimum; add eye, EMG or respiratory channels as useful.
Check impedances and run a calibration and biocal; review the first part of the record for quality.
Stay for an initial period to confirm quality and perform baseline reactivity testing (the consensus describes the first 20 minutes).
Show the RN the event button and how to reach EEG staff; set the camera.

sections.title: Electrode choices and imaging compatibility
head: Option
Use
Notes
rows: Collodion is flammable and needs ventilation; follow facility policy and SDS. Some centers use adhesive paste and covers instead.
Patients likely to be imaged (more than half of cEEG patients need neuroimaging)
Reduce CT streak artifact; MRI use only within the manufacturer's labeling and facility policy.
Very prolonged recording in some centers
May reduce skin breakdown; placement per policy and credentials.
Generally not recommended for prolonged recording and not MRI compatible; sharps and infection precautions.
Rapid set-up or when an NDT is not available

sections.title: Video
items: Time-synchronized video is recommended for ICU cEEG.
Frame the whole body if possible, with the face visible; wall or pole mounting keeps the view stable.
Ask staff not to cover the patient's face and limbs completely; recheck framing after turns and procedures.
Audio is optional but helps identify events and care activities.
Follow facility privacy policy for camera placement and who may view recordings.

sections.title: Quality, impedance and skin checks
head: Check
Frequency in the ACNS consensus
What to do
rows: Look for bad channels, artifact, video framing, correct patient and time.
At least daily, and whenever the recording changes
Consensus calls under 10 kilohms acceptable for cEEG (routine EEG guidelines aim for under 5 kilohms). Re-gel or re-apply as needed.
Look under and around electrodes for redness, breakdown or infection; document and report per written protocol.
At least twice daily (three times for vasospasm)
Daily written report; interim reports for important changes.
sections.note: Many facilities check more often, especially in neonates, edematous or anticoagulated patients, and patients on cooling or pressors.

sections.title: Documentation on the record
items: Patient state, sedation and paralytic drugs with rates; temperature during TTM.
Electrode substitutions, skull defects, drains and incisions.
Each stimulus with time, type, side and observed response.
Nursing care, suctioning, turning, chest physiotherapy, bathing, procedures and transports.
Medication boluses, especially ASMs and sedatives.
Clinical events reported by staff and what the RN saw.
Every notification: who, when, what was reported, per protocol.

pearls: Full 10-20 array (at least 16 electrodes) for standard cEEG; reduced montages are for screening only.
Collodion is preferred for stable long-term electrodes; CT/MRI-compatible electrodes when imaging is likely.
Subdermal needles are not recommended for prolonged recording and are not MRI compatible.
Consensus: impedance under 10 kilohms acceptable; check at least daily and quality at least twice daily.

Always record ECG with ICU EEG; it separates cardiac artifact from cerebral activity.
If an artifact is rhythmic, ask what machine near the patient runs at that rhythm.
tabs.eegLink: A clean ICU record depends on knowing every machine at the bedside and writing down every care activity.

tabs.title: Quantitative EEG Trends
tabs.intro: qEEG trends compress hours of EEG into one screen so changes can be found quickly. They are screening tools: every trend change must be checked on the raw EEG because artifact makes trends lie.

sections.title: Common trends
head: Trend
What it shows
Typical use
rows: Power at each frequency over time, color coded
Seizures often appear as repeated bright 'flames'; slowing shifts power to low frequencies
Filtered, rectified, compressed amplitude band over time
Neonatal background and seizures (seizures often raise the lower margin briefly)
How rhythmic the EEG is at each frequency
Highlights rhythmic patterns and possible seizures
Shows lateralized seizures or new focal slowing
Percent of each epoch that is suppressed
Alpha power divided by delta power
DCI surveillance after SAH; a sustained drop is a warning
How much alpha power fluctuates over time
Loss of variability is a DCI warning sign
Screening aid; false positives and missed seizures both happen

sections.title: Display settings
items: For seizure screening, the consensus suggests trend screens of 2 hours or less, with 30 to 60 minutes preferred.
Short seizures can be missed if the trend averages over long epochs.
For ischemia trends, longer windows (several hours) help show slow changes.
Trends cannot be interpreted in isolation from the raw EEG, and therapy changes should follow review of the raw EEG by the reader.

sections.title: When a trend changes: technologist steps
items: Trend change noticed (flame, asymmetry, BSR shift, ADR drop)
Open the raw EEG at that exact time
Check video, impedance and care log for artifact
Describe what the raw EEG shows and mark it
If a possible seizure, new pattern or sustained change: notify the reader per protocol
Document the time, what was seen and who was notified

cards.title: Muscle and chewing
cards.body: Raise high-frequency power and can look like an arousal or a seizure flame.

cards.title: Patting and bed vibration
cards.body: Rhythmic artifact can create a false rhythmicity or seizure flag.

cards.title: A bad electrode
cards.body: One high-impedance electrode can create a false asymmetry or a fake ADR drop.

cards.title: Sedation changes
cards.body: A propofol bolus can reduce fast activity and change BSR; check the drug log before calling it ischemia or deepening coma.

pearls: qEEG is a screening tool; the raw EEG is the reference.
CSA shows frequency power over time; repeated bright flames suggest seizures.
aEEG is a compressed amplitude band widely used in neonatal ICUs.
BSR is the percent of time suppressed.
Falling ADR after SAH is a DCI warning; check artifact and drug changes first, then notify per protocol.
Seizure trend windows: 30 to 60 minutes preferred, 2 hours or less.
tabs.eegLink: Trends let one technologist watch many patients, but only if every trend alarm is checked on the raw EEG.

tabs.title: Stimulation and Reactivity
tabs.intro: Comatose or sedated patients cannot hyperventilate, look at photic stimulation on command, or open their eyes when asked. Instead, the technologist tests reactivity with a standardized, escalating sequence of stimuli and marks each one carefully.

sections.title: Why standard activation is not possible
items: Hyperventilation needs a cooperative, breathing patient; ventilated patients cannot do it, and changing CO2 in brain injury is a medical decision.
Eye opening and closing on command needs a patient who follows commands.
Photic stimulation is rarely useful in coma and is done only if ordered.
Reactivity testing replaces these: it asks whether the brain's electrical activity changes when the patient is stimulated.

sections.title: Standardized escalating stimulus sequence
items: Check with the RN: sedation and paralytic status, recent care, pain and injuries, anything to avoid (fractures, lines, raised ICP concerns).
Wait for a quiet, settled baseline with no care in progress, and record it before the first stimulus.
Auditory: call the patient's name in a normal voice, then loudly, in each ear; then a loud clap.
Tactile: light touch on the arm or face.
Passive eye opening: gently open the eyes (this also helps identify eye-movement artifact).
Nasal tickle with a cotton swab, if allowed and the nose is free of tubes.
Noxious stimulation per facility policy: for example nail-bed pressure, trapezius squeeze, or sternal rub. Suctioning by the RN can also be used as a stimulus.
Between stimuli, let the EEG return to its baseline before giving the next one.

If no change after one round, a second round of standardized noxious stimulation is suggested (ACNS 2021), starting again from a settled, unstimulated baseline, before the reader calls it unreactive before calling it unreactive.
Repeat testing at the times your protocol sets (for example at hookup and on daily rounds).

sections.title: Marking each stimulus
items: Mark the exact start of each stimulus with type, side and intensity (for example 'loud voice R ear', 'trapezius squeeze L').
Mark what you saw clinically: eye opening, grimace, limb movement, breathing over the vent, heart-rate change, nothing.
Mark care events that act as stimuli (suctioning, turning) even when you did not test.
Without exact marks the reader cannot separate reactivity from chance, or label a pattern SI-.

sections.title: Reactivity, artifact or stimulus-induced pattern
head: What you see after the stimulus
What it is
How to describe it
rows: Change in cerebral voltage or frequency, including attenuation or new faster activity
Describe the change and the stimulus; the reader categorizes it
Only muscle activity or eye-blink artifact
Note the artifact; do not call the EEG reactive
Movement artifact from your hands or the bed
Mark it so the reader does not mistake it
Rhythmic, periodic or ictal-appearing discharges that start or worsen with stimulation
SIRPIDs; patterns get the SI- prefix (for example SI-LPDs, SI-GRDA)
Mark the stimulus and onset; stop that stimulus; notify per protocol if ictal-appearing
A pattern that stops or attenuates with stimulation
Document stimuli, confounders and that testing was adequate
Too much artifact or inadequate testing
Document why testing could not be judged
sections.note: ACNS 2021 reactivity categories: reactive, unreactive, SIRPIDs only, unclear, unknown (not tested, or patient fully alert throughout). The reader assigns them, not the technologist.

cards.title: Sedatives and anesthetics
cards.body: Can reduce or abolish reactivity. Record drugs, doses and the time of the last bolus.

cards.title: Paralytics
cards.body: Remove motor responses and muscle artifact, so you cannot judge clinical arousal; the EEG may still change. Record that the patient is paralyzed.

cards.title: Hypothermia
cards.body: Low temperature slows the EEG and may reduce reactivity; record temperature.

cards.title: Metabolic state and recent seizures
cards.body: Post-ictal state and severe metabolic disturbances can blunt responses; note them.

cards.title: Stimulus artifact
cards.body: Your own movements, the voice of staff, or bed motion can create false changes; keep still leads and note it.

sections.title: Safety, dignity and what not to do
items: Always tell the patient what you are about to do, even if they appear unresponsive; hearing may be preserved.
Coordinate with the RN; explain to family members at the bedside what testing involves.
Use the minimum force needed and the stimuli your facility allows; never cause bruising or skin injury.
Do not use pins, sharp objects or burning stimuli.
Do not stimulate on injured, fractured, burned or surgical areas, or near drains and lines.
Do not test during a seizure or right after a sedative bolus unless the protocol says so; note timing instead.
Do not keep stimulating if stimulation triggers ictal-appearing patterns; mark it and notify per protocol.
Do not call a response 'reactive' because of muscle or eye artifact, and never tell the family what the result means.

pearls: ACNS 2021: reactivity is a change in cerebral EEG activity to stimulation, in voltage or frequency, including attenuation.
Muscle activity or eye-blink artifact alone does not count as reactivity.
Use a standardized, escalating sequence: auditory, tactile, then noxious per protocol.
If unreactive after one round, perform a second round of standardized noxious stimulation.
SIRPIDs are stimulus-induced rhythmic, periodic or ictal-appearing discharges; they are not normal reactivity.
SI- means reproducibly brought on or made worse (exacerbated) by stimulation; ST- means reproducibly terminated or reduced by it.
Record sedation, paralytics and temperature with every test; they change reactivity.
tabs.eegLink: Reactivity and stimulus-induced patterns are only interpretable if every stimulus is standardized and marked with time, type and response.

tabs.title: Reactivity lab
tabs.intro: Three stuporous ICU patients. At the 'Stimulus' mark (5 s) the technologist called the patient's name in a loud voice, one stimulus with its own mark. Compare the settled 5 s before with the 5 s after, and decide what you would document. In practice the protocol continues one stimulus at a time (tactile, then noxious per policy), each marked and followed by a settling pause.

sections.title: Patient 1
sections.question: What does the record show after the stimulus?
options: No change: the background is unreactive
Reactivity: the background attenuates and becomes faster after the stimulus
Muscle artifact only, so reactivity cannot be judged
sections.explanation: Before the mark the background is a mixed theta and delta pattern; after it the overall amplitude drops to roughly half and the slow waves give way to lower-voltage, faster theta, and the change lasts for seconds, beyond the moment of stimulation. A reproducible change in background amplitude or frequency after a stimulus, which is not artifact, is reactivity. Document the stimulus, its time and type, and the change you saw; repeat the stimulus to confirm per protocol.
sections.caption: Background before and after a stimulus.

sections.title: Patient 2
sections.question: What should you document after the stimulus?
options: Reactivity: the background became faster after the stimulus
Generalized periodic discharges appearing after the stimulus (possibly stimulus-induced); mark and notify
Artifact from the nurse's hands on the electrodes
An electrographic seizure, because discharges started
sections.explanation: Before the mark there are no discharges; within about half a second of the stimulus, sharp complexes appear in both hemispheres at about 1 Hz with gaps between them. Periodic discharges brought on by alerting are called stimulus-induced (SIRPIDs; ACNS 2021 prefers naming the specific pattern, for example SI-GPDs). Whether the pattern is SI- depends on it being reproducible with repeated stimulation, and the reader decides. This is not a reactive background, it is not hand artifact because it is generalized and periodic, and it does not meet seizure criteria on this page. Mark the stimulus time and type and notify per protocol.
sections.caption: Discharges appearing after a stimulus.

sections.title: Patient 3
sections.question: How should this response be described?
options: Reactive, because the frontal and temporal channels changed after the stimulus
Stimulus-induced rhythmic delta in the frontal channels
Electrographic seizure in the temporal channels
No EEG change to this stimulus: only brief muscle artifact, with an unchanged background
sections.explanation: Fast, spiky muscle activity appears in the frontopolar and temporal channels for under a second around the stimulus, then the theta-delta background continues unchanged in amplitude and frequency. Artifact caused by the stimulus itself does not count as reactivity, so there is no EEG change to this stimulus. Continue the escalating sequence (tactile, then noxious stimuli per protocol, and a second round from a settled baseline) before reactivity can be judged; the reader assigns the reactivity category. Record sedation, paralytics and temperature, because they can suppress reactivity.
sections.caption: Stimulus with only muscle artifact.

pearls: Mark every stimulus with its time and type: name, loud voice, clap, touch, then the protocol's noxious stimulus.
Wait and watch: compare a stable stretch before with several seconds after.
Artifact from the stimulus is not reactivity.
Discharges that appear after alerting are stimulus-induced (SI-), not reactivity.
Record sedation, paralytics and temperature: they can blunt reactivity.

mistakes: A normal-looking patient on the vent cannot be seizing because nobody sees convulsions.
Most ICU seizures are nonconvulsive, and paralytics hide all motor signs; only the EEG shows them.
A 30 minute routine EEG is enough to rule out seizures in a comatose patient.
Routine EEG misses many NCS; at least 24 h is recommended, 48 h or more if comatose, sedated or with periodic discharges.
'NICU' always means neonatal ICU.
Some hospitals also use it for neuro ICU; confirm before choosing supplies and montage.
Hunt-Hess and mFisher measure the same thing.
Hunt-Hess grades the clinical severity of SAH; mFisher grades the amount of blood on CT.
A few electrodes on the forehead are fine for days of ICU monitoring.
Standard cEEG uses a full 10-20 array of at least 16 electrodes; reduced montages are only for rapid screening.
Subdermal needles are a good choice for multi-day recording and MRI.
Needles are not recommended for prolonged recording and are not MRI compatible; use collodion disks or imaging-compatible electrodes per policy.
A bright flame on the spectrogram is a seizure.
qEEG only screens; check the raw EEG, video and care log for artifact before notifying per protocol.
A falling alpha-delta ratio after SAH should be ignored until the patient gets worse.
A sustained ADR drop or new focal slowing can precede clinical DCI; check artifact and sedation, then notify per protocol.
Eye blinks or a grimace on the EEG after a sternal rub mean the EEG is reactive.
Muscle and eye artifacts do not count; reactivity is a change in cerebral activity.
SIRPIDs show the brain is reacting normally.
SIRPIDs are stimulus-induced rhythmic, periodic or ictal-appearing discharges, a separate category from reactivity.
Give stimuli back to back to save time.
Wait for a settled baseline, give each stimulus in order, let the EEG return to baseline, and mark each with time, type and response.
The technologist can tell the family the EEG shows poor prognosis after cardiac arrest.
Prognosis is the physician's role; the technologist records, describes, marks and notifies per protocol.
